startLeça da Palmeira

Nothing happens at eighteen inches.

Edward Hall measured distance with the body. The line between one zone and the next is not a number. It is the moment you can feel the other's warmth, smell the breath, and the face starts to blur. This page walks toward one building, Siza's tea house on the rocks at Leça da Palmeira, in eight photographs. Each photograph was given to the body and to an image model. Scroll down to approach.

Left column, the body

What I noticed at each distance, written from memory. Wind, sound, smell, floor, glass. The bar above is the body's sense ratio: sight, hearing, smell, skin, muscle, from bright to faint. Press Listen. The sea is synthesized in the browser and follows the notes, louder on the stairs, half under the eaves, low and inside after the door closes.

Right column, the model

The same photograph, resized to the model's input, one caption, one vector. Captions were generated by Claude in one sentence and were not edited. All of them are accurate. Read them again while changing the distance. The kind of sentence never changes.

What falls out of the dataset

Hall's four distances are built from sensory shifts. Sight carries most of the information when the other is far. As you come closer, the ear, the nose, the skin and the muscles take over, one by one. The sense ratio changes, but the total is always one hundred percent.

The model received the same eight photographs. At every distance it returned one sentence and one vector. Nothing got louder. Nothing got colder. The ratio never moved. Its last entry is empty, because no photograph was taken at contact. The last eighteen inches, where Hall says involvement begins, is the part the camera never recorded. It is not in the dataset, and what is not in the dataset falls into what Somaini calls computational oblivion. The latent space is called a space, but no body has ever stood in it.

McLuhan warned that every extension of one sense numbs the others, and that we become what we behold. An archive of buildings made from photographs inherits the sense ratio of the camera. The camera already cut away the sound, the smell and the temperature. The latent space then cuts away even the eye, and keeps only a statistical trace of the image. A model trained on this archive inherits the loss twice. If we keep learning architecture from this archive, we will learn an architecture that can be approached forever without ever getting warmer.
